items.context: The plan adds an `update_policy` JSONB column to `download_apps` for per-app update behavior. We need to settle the default policy shape and values that ship out of the box. This policy will be embedded in the electron-updater config of generated desktop apps.

options.label: Conservative defaults (check every 4 hours, optional updates, no rollback window)
options.rationale: Safest for commercial distribution — users are never forced to update, and the 4-hour interval is standard for electron-updater. No rollback window means simpler logic. Recommended because non-invasive auto-update is a stated goal, and conservative defaults minimize customer friction while still keeping apps current.

options.label: Aggressive defaults (check every 1 hour, mandatory after 7 days, 24h rollback window)
options.rationale: Ensures users stay current quickly. Mandatory flag forces update after grace period. Rollback window adds safety but increases complexity. Better for security-critical apps but may feel invasive for general commercial use.

options.label: Minimal defaults (check on app launch only, optional, no rollback)
options.rationale: Simplest implementation — only check when the app starts, never in the background. Low resource usage but users on long-running sessions may stay on old versions for days.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own default policy shape and values.

items.context: The plan adds `GET /api/v1/updates/{app_key}/channels` to list available channels with latest version per platform. This endpoint could be public (any client can discover channels) or gated behind the same per-app API key used by the update endpoint. Public discovery lets desktop apps auto-discover available channels (e.g., show a 'Switch to beta' option in settings). Gated discovery prevents information leakage about unpublished channels.

options.label: Same gating as update endpoint (public if no update_api_key, gated if set)
options.rationale: Consistent with existing update endpoint behavior. If an app's updates are public, its channel list is too. If gated, the client must provide the same X-Update-Key header. No new auth mechanism needed. Recommended because it follows the principle of least surprise and reuses existing security model.

options.label: Always public (no gating regardless of update_api_key)
options.rationale: Simplifies client implementation — discovery always works without credentials. Channel names are not sensitive (nightly/beta/stable are well-known). But may leak version numbers for unreleased channels.

options.label: Admin-only (requireAdmin middleware)
options.rationale: Maximum security — only admins can see available channels. But desktop apps cannot self-discover channels, which defeats the purpose of the endpoint for client UX.

items.context: The plan adds `is_current` BOOLEAN to `download_assets` to distinguish the active release from historical ones. The question is who sets this flag and when. The research concluded that DM uses application-level 'superseded' status, but LPBS needs its own mechanism since it doesn't depend on DM being present. Currently, `UpsertAsset` does an upsert on (bundle_key, app_key, platform, variant_key) — there's only ever one asset row per slot, so there's no history. Adding `is_current` implies we want to keep old asset rows.

options.label: Keep single-row-per-slot model; add is_current to download_artifacts instead
options.rationale: Assets remain a 1:1 binding (one per app/platform/variant). The artifact table already has multiple rows per app — adding `is_current` there lets us track which artifact is the active one. The asset always points to the current artifact via `artifact_id`. Simpler than changing the asset uniqueness model. Recommended because it preserves the existing asset semantics while enabling version history at the artifact level.

options.label: Remove unique constraint on assets; keep history rows with is_current flag
options.rationale: Full asset-level history — every release creates a new asset row. Richer queryability (list all versions for a platform/channel). But breaks the existing upsert pattern, requires rewriting all asset queries to filter by is_current, and increases query complexity.

options.label: No is_current flag; rely on created_at ordering
options.rationale: Simplest change — 'current' is always the most recently created artifact for a given slot. No schema change needed beyond release_id. But temporal ordering is fragile (clock skew, out-of-order uploads) and doesn't support explicit rollback.

items.context: The plan adds a verification endpoint so that after a release, the S2D pipeline (or an operator) can confirm the update endpoint serves the expected version. The question is what this endpoint checks and what it returns.

options.label: Lightweight version+sha512 check: GET /api/v1/updates/{app_key}/verify?channel=X&platform=Y&expected_version=Z
options.rationale: Checks that the manifest for the given channel/platform reports the expected version and has a non-empty sha512. Returns {match: true/false, actual_version, actual_sha512}. Simple, fast, covers the primary use case of post-deploy smoke testing. Recommended because it's the minimum viable verification that catches the most common failure (wrong version served).

options.label: Deep verification: also validates artifact exists in S3 and presign works
options.rationale: In addition to version matching, actually attempts to generate a presigned URL and HEAD the S3 object. Catches S3 misconfigurations and missing artifacts. More thorough but slower and introduces S3 latency into the verification call.

options.label: Multi-platform batch: POST /api/v1/updates/{app_key}/verify with array of {channel, platform, expected_version}
options.rationale: Verifies all platforms in one call. Better for cross-platform release coordination. But adds request body complexity for what's primarily a smoke test.

items.freeform: Whatever you think is the best long-term solution

items.text: The dependency research (release-record-contract-and-history-model) is completed. It defines the canonical release record schema, channel model, and correlation strategy. This plan incorporates those findings — specifically: release_id as a TEXT correlation column on download_artifacts, parameterized variant_key in UpsertAsset, and channel ordering (nightly → beta → stable). DM-side schema changes (releases table, orchestrator integration) are tracked in separate backlog items under the same initiative.
